events.c: The flight left Rio for Paris with 228 people aboard. The right-seat copilot was flying.
The crew reported passing INTOL and gave estimated arrival times for the next points along the route.
The controller requested an arrival estimate for TASIL. Repeated later requests received no reply.
The aircraft passed SALPU at the edge of radar coverage, marking its last recorded radar position.
A call sounded in the crew rest area before the pilots changed positions.
The relief copilot entered the cockpit. The captain stayed for a briefing before leaving.
The captain left to rest, leaving two copilots at the controls.
The flying copilot warned the cabin crew that more turbulence was expected shortly.
The aircraft began turning left, probably to avoid weather shown on radar.
The crew switched from automatic speed selection to a chosen speed of Mach 0.80.
The crew switched on the system that prevents ice forming on the engine housings.
The autopilot disconnected as speed readings disagreed, likely from ice-blocked sensors. The flying copilot made nose-up control inputs.
The flight-control mode changed, removing automatic protection against the wings losing lift at too steep an angle.
Automatic engine power control disconnected. It and the autopilot remained off for the rest of the flight.
Two brief warnings sounded that the wings could lose lift, before the sustained stall began.
The monitoring copilot identified missing speed readings. The crew did not call for the procedure for unreliable airspeed.
The crew switched on the wing ice-prevention system while the aircraft was climbing.
Nose-up control inputs took the aircraft above its cruising level. Its climb reached 6,900 feet per minute.
The left speed display became reliable after 29 seconds. The backup display remained wrong longer.
The warning of lost wing lift became continuous. The flying copilot continued mainly nose-up control inputs.
A call chime sounded for the cabin or crew rest area. Further calls went to the rest area.
Vibration became audible in the cockpit as the aircraft approached a loss of wing lift.
The crew selected takeoff engine power, but the wing's angle to the airflow kept rising before the descent.
The main and backup speed readings agreed again as the aircraft neared the top of its climb.
The highest altitude reading reached about 38,000 feet. Its exact height above sea level is unknown.
The copilots briefly switched control priority between them without clear spoken handovers.
The captain returned during the stalled descent. The crew did not agree that the wings had lost lift.
The stall warning stopped when sensor readings became invalid. The aircraft had not recovered.
The crew moved the engine power levers to idle. Engine power then decreased.
The crew briefly deployed the aircraft's air brakes for about three seconds.
The crew selected climb power. The engines responded by increasing power.
The right-seat copilot briefly pushed fully forward and selected takeoff power. Later readings still showed stalled wings.
The altitude display read about 10,000 feet. The flying copilot mentioned approaching that level.
Both copilots made overlapping inputs, with the left mostly commanding nose-down and the right alternating nose-up and neutral.
The crew briefly reduced engine power to idle, then increased it and later moved toward takeoff power again.
Warnings sounded about rapid descent and the need to pull up, about 2,140 feet above the sea.
The wing's angle to the airflow remained steep. The right-seat copilot took control priority until the flight ended.
The recording ended near ocean impact. The aircraft remained intact until impact, descending rapidly with its nose raised.
Rescue coordination began gathering flight information. Failures in monitoring and coordination delayed alerts and search deployment.
French and Brazilian forces began recovering wreckage and victims from the sea on June 6.
A new search map combined likely aircraft movements, uncertain drift estimates, and earlier unsuccessful searches to locate wreckage.
The main wreckage was found about 3,900 meters below the sea. The exact discovery date is uncertain.
The flight recorder's protected memory unit was recovered from the seabed, a day after it was found.
The cockpit voice recorder was recovered. Both recorders were later read in France.
The investigation linked faulty speed readings, control inputs, and an unrecognized stall, identifying training and crew-coordination weaknesses.
Airbus and Air France were acquitted at the first criminal trial. The acquittals were later reversed on appeal.
The appeal hearings began on September 29, 2025, and continued through November 27.
The appeal court convicted Airbus and Air France of involuntary homicide, fining each company €225,000.
Airbus announced plans to seek a further court review. The outcome is unknown.

numbers.label: Continuous warning of lost wing lift

one_line: Unreliable speed readings preceded loss of control, a sustained loss of wing lift, and ocean impact.
status_why: Recovered recorders establish the loss of control and stall sequence, while corporate legal responsibility remains contested.
